question: Who of the following Chola rulers initially occupied the northern part of Sri Lanka in his raids?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Rajaraja I**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Rajaraja I**, also known as Rajaraja the Great, was one of the most prominent Chola rulers in South Indian history.
 
• He conducted successful military campaigns in Sri Lanka, initially occupying the northern part of the island, including Jaffna.
 
• The conquest of northern Sri Lanka by Rajaraja I occurred around **AD 993**, during his reign.
 
• The region was named "Mummudi Chola Mandalam" after its annexation, symbolizing the Chola authority over the island.
 
• This expansion under Rajaraja I marked the beginning of the Chola influence in Sri Lanka, which was further consolidated by his successors.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **The Chola Dynasty:**

 
 
• The Cholas were a prominent Tamil dynasty that ruled over South India and parts of Southeast Asia from the 9th to 13th century AD.
 
• They are renowned for their contributions to art, architecture, administration, and maritime trade.
 
 
 
• **Rajaraja I's Achievements:**
 
 
• He was responsible for constructing the famous **Brihadeeswarar Temple** in Thanjavur, a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
 
• Rajaraja I also expanded the Chola Navy, facilitating overseas expeditions and trade.
 
 
 
• **Chola Administration:**
 
 
• The Cholas implemented an efficient administrative system, including well-organized local self-governance in villages.
 
• Their inscriptions provide valuable information about their governance and socio-economic conditions.
 
 
 
• **Chola Expansion in Sri Lanka:**
 
 
• Following Rajaraja I's conquest, his son **Rajendra I** further expanded Chola influence in Sri Lanka, eventually capturing the entire island.
 
• These campaigns were driven by strategic and economic motives, including control over trade routes.
